claims.statement: Convergence is one shared step that every read path calls before answering — every MCP read tool and every read CLI subcommand — rather than a per-caller reimplementation, and it is what lets a note committed a moment ago be recall-able on the next read with no manual reindex.

A convergence pass is ordered as debounce check, non-blocking lock acquisition, optional authoring-host overlay, delta sizing, lexical delta replay that advances the checkpoint, a bounded dense fill, and a debounce stamp write.
The debounce check short-circuits before any lock is taken, using a timestamp stored in the index state directory, so a burst of reads pays the catch-up cost once.

Convergence takes the single-indexer lock non-blocking and, when another writer or converger holds it, returns immediately serving the current state — so a read never stalls behind an in-progress index advance.
Convergence writes only the index state directory and never the repository, so a read path can never mutate the source of truth.

The convergence result's status discriminates four operationally distinct outcomes — converged, debounced, lock_busy, and oversized_delta — alongside counts of replayed paths and embedded chunks and doc surfaces, the degraded flag and reason, overlay paths, the observed HEAD, and whether the checkpoint advanced.

Convergence is delta-replay plus a bounded embed and never invokes the isolated full-rebuild path, keeping full reindex a manual explicit operation so a read can never trigger an unbounded rebuild that exhausts memory on a large vault.

A delta larger than the configured file cap is not replayed inline because a partial replay could not advance the checkpoint to HEAD and every subsequent read would recompute the same delta with no progress; convergence instead serves the current consistent projection and recommends a manual reindex.
The manual-reindex recommendation is a signal surfaced in every read result rather than an action: nothing rebuilds itself and the caller decides.

Convergence never raises on the read path: with no embedder or a failing one the lexical and graph catch-up still completes and the checkpoint still advances, with only the dense fill skipped and the result flagged degraded with a named reason such as a missing embedder or the embedding error's own reason.
The checkpoint advances on the lexical replay, which is precisely why a later dense failure is a degradation rather than a rollback of the pass.
A partially completed embedding batch leaves real vectors rather than zero placeholders, because a zero-filled vector silently participates in ranking and is worse than a missing one.

The authoring-host overlay indexes uncommitted and untracked markdown so in-progress notes are findable before commit, but it is lexical only with its paths excluded from the dense fill and it never advances the checkpoint, so a replica projecting the same committed SHA sees none of it.
The overlay is best-effort: if git is unavailable or the status call fails, convergence continues without the overlay rather than failing the read.
Delta replay reads each changed file's content from the commit object rather than from the working tree, which is what makes the index a projection of HEAD rather than of a possibly dirty checkout.

When reading a changed file from git fails — a missing, pruned, or corrupt object — the path's existing index rows are left intact rather than being overwritten with empty content, so a transient git failure degrades to staleness rather than blanking a note.
Every convergence tunable is injectable per call rather than read only from module configuration, which is how tests make each path deterministic — for example by disabling the debounce.

Convergence is additionally triggered outside reads by an explicit converge subcommand used as a manual pre-warm and by the opt-in post-merge git hook, so a pull warms the index instead of leaving the cost to the next reader.
